title.rendered: What Is a Good Conversion Rate on Shopify?

content.rendered:
[vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”3″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310001″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”310002″]The short answer[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310003″]A good conversion rate on Shopify is anything above 3.2%. That puts a store in the top 20%. The platform average is 1.4%, and above 4.7% puts you in the top 10%.

Those figures come from Littledata’s benchmark of 2,800 Shopify stores. They are a useful yardstick and a poor target, because your sector, your price point, your device mix and where your traffic comes from move the number more than anything on your site does.[/vc_column_text][vc_custom_heading heading_semantic=”h3″ text_size=”h3″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310004″]Key takeaways[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310005″]

  • The average Shopify conversion rate is 1.4%. Above 3.2% is the top 20%, above 4.7% is the top 10%.
  • Mobile converts at 1.2% against 1.9% on desktop, and mobile is where most of the traffic sits.
  • UK and Irish independent merchants averaged 2.23% in August 2026, up from 1.85% a year earlier, on 13.69% fewer visitors.
  • Sector moves the number more than tactics do. Food and drink averaged 1.58% in August 2026, arts and crafts 5.81%.
  • A realistic target is a 10% to 30% relative improvement over a few months, not a doubling.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310010″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”310011″]What is a good conversion rate on Shopify?[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”667594″]Above 3.2% is good and above 4.7% is excellent. The average sits at 1.4%. These are Littledata’s Shopify-specific percentiles, taken from a benchmark of 2,800 stores, and they are the only widely published benchmark measuring Shopify on its own rather than ecommerce as a whole.

Performance Shopify conversion rate
Average 1.4%
Top 20% Above 3.2%
Top 10% Above 4.7%
Average, mobile 1.2%
Average, desktop 1.9%
Top 10%, mobile Above 3.9%
Top 10%, desktop Above 6.5%

Source: Littledata.

One caveat, because most articles quoting these numbers leave it out. Littledata’s benchmark is a 2023 dataset. It is still the most recent Shopify-only benchmark published anywhere, which is why everyone cites it, but it is not this year’s number. If you find a page quoting an updated Littledata study across several thousand more stores, check it against Littledata’s own page before you trust it.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310020″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”310021″]Does a good conversion rate depend on your sector?[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”114986″]Yes, and more than most brands expect. In August 2026, arts and crafts stores across the UK and Ireland averaged 5.81% while baby and child averaged 0.57%. That is a tenfold spread inside the same month and the same dataset.

Sector Aug 2026 Aug 2025
Arts and crafts 5.81% 4.00%
Health and wellbeing 3.31% 3.30%
Kitchen and home appliances 2.98% 3.47%
Pet care 2.56% 2.62%
All markets 2.23% 1.85%
Sports and recreation 2.11% 1.57%
Cars and motorcycling 1.86% 1.27%
Fashion, clothing and accessories 1.86% 1.45%
Toys, games and collectables 1.64% 2.03%
Food and drink 1.58% 1.16%
Baby and child 0.57% 0.62%

Source: IRP Commerce, August 2026.

Two things sit underneath any sector average. The first is price point. Lower priced, repeat purchase products convert higher, and considered purchases always convert lower because people research, compare and come back. Baby and child makes the point. It has the lowest conversion rate in the table at 0.57%, but an average order value of £855.57 and an average item price of £665.15, which points to big-ticket purchases like prams and nursery furniture. Each session there is worth £5.01, against £1.92 across all markets.

The second is traffic source. Returning customers convert far better than cold paid traffic, so scaling acquisition usually drags the headline rate down even when the site itself is performing better. The same sector fits that pattern. Its visitor numbers rose 57.89% year on year while its conversion rate fell, and acquisition costs rose 26.83%, the second steepest increase of any sector.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310030″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”310031″]Why is your mobile conversion rate lower than desktop?[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310032″]Because most stores are still designed for desktop and then squeezed onto a phone. On Shopify, mobile averages 1.2% against 1.9% on desktop. The gap widens at the top, where the best 10% of stores manage more than 3.9% on mobile and more than 6.5% on desktop.

That matters because mobile is where the traffic is. In August 2026, mobile accounted for 63.7% of sales across UK and Irish independent merchants, desktop 34.7% and tablet 1.6%. If your mobile rate sits far below your desktop rate, the losses are concentrated on the majority of your visits.

The fix is rarely a mobile-specific patch bolted on at the end. It is designing the journey for a phone first and letting the desktop version inherit it.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310040″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”310041″]Are you measuring the same number as the benchmark?[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310042″]Almost every published benchmark counts sessions, not people. Conversion rate is transactions divided by sessions, multiplied by 100. If your own figure counts unique visitors instead, it will read higher for the same store, and comparing it to a session-based benchmark will flatter you.

IRP Commerce states its calculation openly: transactions divided by sessions, times 100. Littledata’s Shopify figures are session based too. Your Shopify dashboard reports by session, and GA4 can give you a different number again depending on how it has been set up.

Bot traffic is the other trap. Inflated session counts push a reported conversion rate down without anything changing on the site. I have worked on stores where the analytics were unusable for year-on-year comparison for that exact reason, and the only honest option was to benchmark against order data instead.

Before you decide your rate is poor, check you are comparing like with like.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310050″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”310051″]Why is your conversion rate below the benchmark?[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310052″]Usually it is not one broken thing. It is friction spread thinly across the journey.

Discovery is the first leak. If people cannot find the right product quickly they leave before they ever reach a product page, and large catalogues suffer most, because a stock theme menu was never built for thousands of products.

The product card is the second. People decide on collection pages far more than most brands realise, so a card that does not answer the question driving the decision forces everyone into a product page they did not need to open.

The third is cost surprise. Unclear delivery thresholds and charges that appear late kill more sales than any design detail.

I have written separately about the practical fixes.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310060″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”310061″]What actually moves the number?[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310062″]This is the part I can speak to from projects rather than theory.[/vc_column_text][vc_empty_space empty_h=”2″][vc_custom_heading heading_semantic=”h3″ text_size=”h3″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310063″]Design the collection page around the decision[/vc_custom_heading][vc_single_image media=”162182″ media_width_percent=”100″ alignment=”center” shape=”img-round” radius=”std” advanced=”yes” media_items=”media|original,spacer|half,caption” media_overlay_opacity=”50″ media_overlay_anim=”no” media_text_anim=”no” media_image_anim=”no” media_padding=”2″ uncode_shortcode_id=”594305″][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310064″]On East at Home, a DTC food brand, the collection pages were rebuilt around bespoke product cards that surface what actually drives the choice: spice level, dietary fit, flavour. A customer can compare the range without opening a single product page.

Conversion rate rose 14% from a base that was already well above sector average, and revenue grew 82% year on year.

Read the East at Home case study[/vc_column_text][vc_empty_space empty_h=”2″][vc_custom_heading heading_semantic=”h3″ text_size=”h3″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310065″]Let people compare without leaving the listing[/vc_custom_heading][vc_single_image media=”162181″ media_width_percent=”100″ alignment=”center” shape=”img-round” radius=”std” advanced=”yes” media_items=”media|original,spacer|half,caption” media_overlay_opacity=”50″ media_overlay_anim=”no” media_text_anim=”no” media_image_anim=”no” media_padding=”2″ uncode_shortcode_id=”194197″][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310066″]Drink Finder is a Cornish wine and spirits merchant with more than 5,000 products. I designed a comparison toggle that expands details like origin and age inside the listing, so shoppers can weigh bottles side by side before opening anything.

In a category where people compare constantly, that changed the browsing experience entirely. Website sales grew 34% and customer numbers grew 32% year on year, in a period when the premium drinks market was contracting.

Read the Drink Finder case study[/vc_column_text][vc_empty_space empty_h=”2″][vc_custom_heading heading_semantic=”h3″ text_size=”h3″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310067″]Make the value of buying more visible at the moment of decision[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310068″]Rather than fixed bundle variants, a quantity selector that recalculates the total, the saving and the price per unit live as the customer adjusts the amount. A basket progress bar shows what each threshold unlocks.

No countdown timers and no artificial scarcity anywhere in it. Order value rose through clarity.[/vc_column_text][vc_empty_space empty_h=”2″][vc_custom_heading heading_semantic=”h3″ text_size=”h3″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310069″]Build navigation for the catalogue you actually have[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310070″]A theme’s default menu will not cope with thousands of products. On the drinks project the mobile navigation was built from scratch rather than bent out of a generic component, and a catalogue that had been a barrier became calm to browse. Checkout starts rose 23% and add to basket actions rose 27%.[/vc_column_text][vc_empty_space empty_h=”2″][vc_custom_heading heading_semantic=”h3″ text_size=”h3″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310071″]Map the journey before designing anything[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310072″]Every one of those decisions came out of reviewing the purchase journey rather than instinct. The whole journey gets mapped, each step flagged where customers hesitate, and only then does design start. That is what a Shopify UX review is for.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310080″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”310081″]What does not work?[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310082″]Countdown timers and manufactured scarcity. They cost trust, and the lift fades as soon as customers recognise the pattern.

Discounting to fix a conversion problem. It hides the problem and teaches customers to wait.

Redesigning because the site looks dated. If you cannot say which step in the journey is losing people, a redesign is a gamble rather than a fix.

Copying a competitor’s layout. Their layout suits their catalogue, their price point and their customers.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310090″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”310091″]How much improvement is realistic?[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310092″]A 10% to 30% relative improvement over a few months is a good outcome for most stores. Moving from 1.5% to 1.8% sounds unremarkable and is worth a great deal of money on the same traffic.

Be sceptical of anyone promising to double it. Stores that see enormous jumps usually had something badly broken rather than something that needed optimising.

Allow four to six weeks after a change before judging the result, and longer if your traffic is modest. The market moves as well. Across UK and Irish independent merchants, visitor numbers fell 13.69% year on year in August 2026 while conversion rose 20.49% and revenue per session rose 24.65%. Fewer people are arriving and the ones who do are worth more. A store that only held flat against that was not standing still.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”310100″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”310101″]Where to start[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”310102″]A good Shopify conversion rate is above 3.2%, the average is 1.4%, and the top 10% clear 4.7%. None of those numbers means much until you account for your sector, your price point and your device mix, which is why the most useful benchmark is your own previous period.

Measure your rate by device and by traffic source before you measure it against anyone else. One blended number hides the problem. Split it and it usually points straight at it.

If you want it looked at properly, that is the work I do with DTC brands. mainEntity.name: What is the average conversion rate on Shopify?

acceptedAnswer.text: 1.4% across all stores, according to Littledata's benchmark of 2,800 Shopify sites. Mobile averages 1.2% and desktop 1.9%. Sector and price point cause enormous variation, so treat the average as a reference point rather than a target.

mainEntity.name: Is 2% a good conversion rate on Shopify?

acceptedAnswer.text: 2% is above the Shopify average of 1.4% and below the 3.2% that marks the top 20%. Whether it is good for your store depends on your sector, your price point and how much of your traffic is cold and paid.

mainEntity.name: How is a Shopify conversion rate calculated?

acceptedAnswer.text: Transactions divided by sessions, multiplied by 100. Sessions, not unique visitors. A visitor-based figure reads higher for the same store, so check which one a benchmark uses before comparing yourself to it.

mainEntity.name: Why is my mobile conversion rate lower than my desktop rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: That is normal. On Shopify, mobile averages 1.2% against 1.9% on desktop. A very large gap usually means the site was designed desktop first and squeezed down. Since mobile carries most of the traffic, closing that gap is often the single biggest opportunity.

mainEntity.name: What is a good conversion rate for a UK store?

acceptedAnswer.text: Across UK and Irish independent merchants the average session conversion rate was 2.23% in August 2026, up from 1.85% a year earlier, according to IRP Commerce. That figure covers all platforms rather than Shopify alone, and it varies sharply by sector.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to improve a Shopify conversion rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Allow four to six weeks after a change before the data means anything, and longer on modest traffic. A realistic outcome is a 10% to 30% relative improvement over a few months rather than a sudden jump.

[vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”3″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”202009″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”500401″]Two projects, one independent designer[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”955526″]I won UK eCommerce Website of the Year and UK User Experience of the Year at the UK eCommerce Awards 2026, for my work with Drink Finder and East at Home. I was the only independent designer on the shortlist. Every other entry was an agency, a brand or a technology company. Both of these projects were designed by one person working directly with the client, which is exactly how I prefer to work. I am a freelance Shopify designer based in Falmouth, Cornwall.

Below is the work behind each win, and the two other categories the projects were shortlisted in.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”207802″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”213702″]UK eCommerce Website of the Year: Drink Finder[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”366901″]Drink Finder won UK eCommerce Website of the Year 2026. It is an independent Cornish wine and spirits merchant trading for 65 years, with more than 5,000 products across retail, wholesale and trade. Migrating a catalogue that size to Shopify carried real risk.

I designed the entire purchase journey mobile-first before any development began. Bespoke navigation built from scratch so a very large range stays browsable on a phone, a comparison toggle so customers can weigh bottles side by side, and a rebuilt product page and checkout.

Website sales grew 34% and customer numbers grew 32% year on year, in a period when the premium drinks market contracted.

Read the Drink Finder case study[/vc_column_text][vc_single_image media=”162162″ media_width_percent=”100″ alignment=”center” shape=”img-round” radius=”std” advanced=”yes” media_overlay_opacity=”50″ media_overlay_anim=”no” media_text_anim=”no” media_image_anim=”no” media_padding=”2″ uncode_shortcode_id=”144274″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”207803″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”213703″]Why this award matters[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”366902″]UK eCommerce Website of the Year is the overall award. Rather than judging one sector, the judges compare websites from every category to pick a single winner, and the shortlist included national retailers and household names.

What made this one worth entering was the scale of the challenge rather than the scale of the business. A 65 year old independent merchant, a catalogue in the thousands, three separate customer types to serve, and a platform migration that had to happen without losing the customers who had shopped there for years.

The design work had to hold all of that together and still feel like a premium drinks retailer rather than a database.

More on Shopify migration[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”207804″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”213704″]UK User Experience of the Year: East at Home[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”366903″]East at Home, a DTC food brand making restaurant quality curries achievable at home, won UK User Experience of the Year 2026.

This was a harder brief than a typical redesign, because the existing site already converted well above sector average. The risk was breaking what worked. So every decision came out of a full review of the purchase journey, mapping where customers hesitated rather than guessing, and the product experience was rebuilt mobile-first around how people actually decide what to cook.

A bespoke quantity selector makes the value of buying more visible at the exact moment of decision. The product card answers the questions people ask before they click, so the journey into the product page becomes optional rather than mandatory. There are no countdown timers, no discount pressure and no dark patterns anywhere in it.

Conversion rate rose 14% from an already strong base, and revenue grew 82% year on year. The gains came from clarity, and that is the part I am most pleased to see recognised.

Read the East at Home case study[/vc_column_text][vc_single_image media=”162163″ media_width_percent=”100″ alignment=”center” shape=”img-round” radius=”std” advanced=”yes” media_overlay_opacity=”50″ media_overlay_anim=”no” media_text_anim=”no” media_image_anim=”no” media_padding=”2″ uncode_shortcode_id=”723322″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”207805″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”213705″]Also shortlisted[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”366904″]Both projects were also finalists in a second category. Drink Finder was shortlisted for Food & Drink eCommerce Website of the Year, and East at Home for B2C eCommerce Website of the Year. Four shortlistings from two projects, and a win for each.

See all my Shopify case studies[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”390801″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”962701″]Why more freelancers should enter[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”506301″]I suspect a lot of freelancers are put off entering awards. A submission takes real time, that time is not billable, and there is an entry fee on top. When you are running everything yourself, all three of those are easy reasons to leave it another year.

Two wins later, I am glad I did not. I am proud of the work I have been doing since going freelance, and I know how good these two projects are. Not only from a design point of view, but commercially. Both were built to sell, and both do.

That is the case I would make to any other freelancer weighing it up. If the work is good and the results are there, the size of the studio behind it does not change the quality of what was made.

Drink Finder won UK eCommerce Website of the Year and East at Home won UK User Experience of the Year. [vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”3″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”202009″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”500113″]Introduction[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”118379″]If you have ever hired a designer or an agency for a Shopify project, you have probably been through a discovery phase. For many agencies, that involves filling out a brief, building user personas, and running a workshop or two before the design work starts. The output is a deck of imagined customers with names like Sarah the busy mum and assumed shopping habits that nobody has ever actually validated.

I do it differently. Every Shopify project I take on starts with a UX review based on real data and the live store as it actually exists, not assumptions about who the customers might be or what they might want. This article walks through what that looks like, why it matters, and what comes out the other end.

I am Anthony, a UK Shopify expert specialising in design and Shopify CRO for ambitious DTC brands. The UX review process I am about to describe is the one I have refined over years of agency work and freelance projects. It is how every engagement begins.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”207832″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”212043″]What is a Shopify UX review?[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”803667″]A Shopify UX review is a structured analysis of how customers actually use a live Shopify store, combining real analytics data with a designer’s expert eye to identify where the experience is helping conversion and where it is hurting it. It covers the full purchase journey from landing on the site to completing checkout, flags both what is working and what is not, and produces a clear set of recommendations for what to change first.

Three things distinguish a good UX review from a generic ecommerce audit:

  • Real data, not assumptions. Real users in GA4, not invented personas. Real device and screen size data, not generic best practice.
  • Designer judgement on top of the numbers. The data tells you what is happening. A designer’s eye tells you why and what to do about it. Neither alone is enough.
  • Balance between good and bad. A good UX review flags what is working as well as what is not. This is not a hatchet job. It is a clear-eyed assessment of an existing store from someone who wants the project to succeed.

Real devices, real time, real expertise

A proper UX review is not done in a browser window with the device emulator turned on. The review has to be done on the actual devices customers are using. I go through the store on real phones, real tablets, and real desktops, in the same way customers do. Browser emulators are useful for quick checks but they miss the real-world friction. The way a button responds to an actual thumb on an actual phone is different to how it looks in DevTools. The way text wraps on a real Samsung is different to how Chrome renders it. The way an iOS form keyboard behaves over the page is different to what the emulator shows.

Time matters too. A UX review done properly takes days, not hours. The GA4 analysis alone is a serious piece of work, the Miro purchase journey mapping has to be done screen by screen at the right viewport sizes, and the heuristic review needs to be unhurried so that nothing gets missed. There is no shortcut to this. Anyone offering a comprehensive UX review in an hour is not doing the work.

And expertise matters most of all. The reason I can do this work is not because I own a Miro account and have access to GA4. Those tools are public, anyone can use them. What makes the review valuable is 20+ years of design experience, six years of that focused exclusively on Shopify, and the judgement that comes from having designed for fragrance brands, food brands, wine retailers, pet food subscriptions, greeting card publishers, footwear, and bespoke bookbinders. The tools help me put the review together. The thinking behind it is what makes it useful.

Why a paid UX review is different to a free site audit

Most Shopify agencies offer free site audits as a way to start a sales conversation. These are not the same thing as a UX review and should not be confused with one. A free audit is typically a 15-minute skim through the site, often run through automated tools, producing a generic checklist of issues that look serious on a slide but are usually surface-level. Page speed, missing meta tags, generic mobile responsiveness flags. The same audit could be produced for any Shopify store. There is no time invested, no real data behind it, and no design judgement applied.

That is fine for what it is — a lead generation tactic. It is not what I do. A paid UX review is days of work, grounded in your store’s real users, mapped against your store’s real purchase journey, applied to your store’s specific products and customers. The deliverables are real working documents that inform months of design and development decisions, not a slide deck designed to make you sign a contract. The difference is not subtle, and the value is not comparable.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”112906″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”117598″]Why made-up personas are a worse way to start a project[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”147091″]Personas are a discovery-phase staple for many agencies. The team gets together in a room, looks at the client’s brief, and builds a few imagined customers. Sarah the busy mum, James the gadget enthusiast, Priya the considered shopper. Each persona gets a fictional age, location, set of pain points, and shopping behaviours.

The problem with this approach is that it is entirely made up. None of those people exist. None of their pain points have been validated against real customer behaviour. The team has spent half a day inventing assumptions, which are then presented to the client as insight, and the design work that follows is built on those assumptions rather than on anything real.

I am not saying personas have no place in the design world. For brand-new products with no customers yet, they can be a starting point because there is no real data to work from. But for an established Shopify store with real customers, real analytics, and a real purchase journey already running, choosing imagined users over real ones is a strange decision. The data is already there. The customers are already there. Looking at imagined ones first is throwing away the most valuable input the project has.

Looking back at some of the persona-led discovery work I have been involved in over my career, I have come to think of it as a comfort blanket for agencies. It produces a tidy deliverable, it fills a chargeable phase of the project, and it gives the design team the feeling that they understand the user. But the understanding is fictional. The customers in the persona deck have never set foot on the client’s site. The real customers have. Why would you start with the wrong group?[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”791020″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”823010″]Stage one: the GA4 data analysis[/vc_custom_heading][vc_single_image media=”161496″ caption=”yes” media_width_percent=”100″ shape=”img-round” radius=”std” advanced=”yes” media_overlay_opacity=”50″ media_overlay_anim=”no” media_text_anim=”no” media_image_anim=”no” media_padding=”2″ uncode_shortcode_id=”613929″][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”124726″]The first stage of every UX review is a topline analytics review using GA4. The goal at this stage is not to dive into every metric or replicate the work of an SEO specialist. The goal is to understand who is using the store, on what devices, on which pages, and where they drop out of the purchase journey. That information then shapes what comes next.

The standard reports I look at for every Shopify UX review include:

  • Traffic Acquisition and Channel. Where is traffic coming from? Organic search, paid, email, direct, referral. The mix tells me what kind of customer is landing on the site and what their intent likely is.
  • Landing pages. Which pages are people entering on? The homepage rarely dominates as much as clients expect. Product pages and collection pages often get more entry traffic, which changes which pages matter most in the redesign.
  • Pages and Screens. Which pages get the most engagement, and how long do visitors spend on each? Patterns here often surface unexpected priorities.
  • Organic Search queries and pages. What are customers actually searching for to find the site, and which pages do they land on? This often exposes intent that the existing site is not serving well.
  • User Demographics. Country, language, age where available. UK-focused brands sometimes find significant overseas traffic they have not designed for.
  • Tech (device, OS, browser). The mobile / desktop / tablet split is the headline number, but the breakdown across operating systems and browsers matters too. A brand with heavy iOS traffic needs to design for Safari quirks. A brand with significant older-Android usage needs to design for slower devices.
  • Resolution by revenue. Which screen sizes actually drive sales? This often differs from which screen sizes get the most traffic. It tells me which mobile viewport widths to design for first.
  • Purchase Journey. The full funnel from product view to add to cart to checkout to purchase. The drop-off between each step is where the design work needs to focus.
  • Ecommerce purchases and conversion rate. The baseline. The number we want to improve, broken down by device, by traffic source, and by product where useful.

This stage produces a topline picture of the store. It is not a deep analytics dive — that is a separate piece of work, and there are SEO and CRO specialists who go far deeper into the data than I do. The goal at this point is to know enough about the real users to design properly for them. That means knowing what devices to design for, which pages matter most, and where in the funnel customers are dropping out.

It also surfaces anomalies. Every store has them. A page that gets unexpectedly high traffic, a device split that is heavier mobile than the client realised, a conversion rate that drops off a cliff on a specific viewport. Anomalies are some of the most valuable starting points for a project, and they almost always lead to a useful conversation with the client about what is going on and why.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”791020″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”194660″]Stage two: the Miro purchase journey mapping[/vc_custom_heading][vc_single_image media=”146501″ caption=”yes” media_width_percent=”100″ shape=”img-round” radius=”std” advanced=”yes” advanced_videos=”yes” media_overlay_opacity=”50″ media_overlay_anim=”no” media_text_anim=”no” media_image_anim=”no” media_padding=”2″ mobile_videos=”autoplay” uncode_shortcode_id=”175540″][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”949573″]Once I have the data picture, I take the most important screens of the actual purchase journey and map them in Miro. Homepage. Collection page. Product page. Cart. Checkout. Plus any specific pages flagged by the data, like a high-traffic blog article or an unexpected landing page.

Each screen is mapped at the actual screen sizes that the data has told me matter most, and reviewed on the actual devices customers are using. A brand with heavy mobile revenue gets the mobile journey mapped first, walked through on real phones. A B2B brand with desktop-heavy traffic gets desktop. The point is to look at the experience the real customers are actually seeing, not a generic representative screenshot.

Every screen is then annotated with colour-coded post-it notes:

  • Green — Good. What is working on this screen. Trust signals, clear hierarchy, strong product imagery, smooth interactions. These get flagged because they are worth keeping and worth understanding before redesigning anything.
  • Yellow — Note. Observations that are neither obviously good nor bad. Things worth flagging for discussion with the client, or patterns that need more context before a recommendation can be made.
  • Orange — Bad. Problems and roadblocks. UI conflicts, broken hierarchy, missing trust signals, friction points, accessibility issues, anything actively hurting the customer experience.
  • Blue — Suggestion or Solution. Where I propose what to do about a problem, either tactically (move this button up here) or strategically (this whole section needs a new layout).

There is also a fold line on each mobile screen, showing where the content drops below the visible area on common viewports. This often surfaces issues clients had not noticed, because the design team and the client always look at the full page on a desktop monitor. The actual customer on a phone might never see what is below the fold.[/vc_column_text][vc_single_image media=”146554″ caption=”yes” media_width_percent=”100″ shape=”img-round” radius=”std” advanced=”yes” advanced_videos=”yes” media_overlay_opacity=”50″ media_overlay_anim=”no” media_text_anim=”no” media_image_anim=”no” media_padding=”2″ mobile_videos=”autoplay” uncode_shortcode_id=”821855″][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”191819″]The key principle is balance. The board flags good as well as bad. Most UX audits I have seen only mark the problems, which produces a demoralising deliverable and gives the client the impression their site is a complete write-off. It rarely is. Every Shopify store has elements that are working, and identifying them is just as important as finding the things that are not. Keep what works, improve what does not. That is the brief in five words.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”791020″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”567234″]Stage three: the heuristic design review[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”204545″]The third stage is the bit that data alone cannot do. It is design judgement applied to the live store. Things like:

  • Whether the brand is being expressed properly across the site, or whether it falls apart on collection and product pages
  • Whether the typography hierarchy is doing its job at every viewport
  • Whether the product imagery is consistent, on-brand, and doing the work it needs to
  • Whether the buttons, forms, and interactive elements feel as considered as the rest of the design
  • Whether the mobile experience feels like an afterthought or a first-class design
  • Whether the brand has earned the customer’s trust by the time they reach the checkout

This is where 20+ years of design experience does its work. The GA4 data tells me what is happening, the Miro board tells me where in the journey it is happening, and the heuristic review tells me why and what should be done about it. None of those three stages alone is enough. Together they produce a UX review that is grounded in real users, mapped against the real journey, and informed by real design judgement.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”791020″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”170166″]What comes out of a Shopify UX review[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”155042″]There are two deliverables at the end of a UX review.

1. The Miro board

The first is the Miro board itself. It is shared with the client and they keep it. Once the review is complete, the board becomes a working document the team can refer back to throughout the project. Every design decision that follows can be traced back to a flagged issue on the board, which keeps everyone honest about what the work is supposed to fix.

Because the board is shared, the client also has the option of making some adjustments themselves in the Shopify theme customiser before the design work begins. Small fixes — copy tweaks, settings adjustments, content reorganisation — can often be done in the customiser without any design or development work, and ticking those off early means the design budget can focus on the bigger structural changes. It is a practical, generous way to start a project rather than an artificial bottleneck where nothing happens until everything is signed off.

2. The to-do list with design and development time allocations

The second deliverable is a clear to-do list, usually as a Word or Excel document, that turns the Miro board’s findings into a structured list of actions. Each item has a column for the design time it would take, and a separate column for the development time. Some items are design-only changes the customiser can handle without development. Others are design changes that need development to implement. A few are pure development tasks that do not need fresh design work. The to-do list makes all of that transparent.

This gives the client real control over what gets done first. They can look at the full list, see the time investment behind each item, and tell me which areas to prioritise based on their budget and their commercial priorities. Some clients want to focus on the highest-conversion-impact items first. Others want to start with the lowest-hanging fruit to show momentum to their team. The to-do list lets us have that conversation properly, with the numbers in front of us, rather than guessing.

It also makes the project scope honest. The client knows exactly what they are paying for, exactly how long each piece will take, and exactly what is and is not in scope. Surprises late in the project are usually a sign of bad scoping at the beginning, and the to-do list eliminates most of the room for that.

From there, the project moves into design proper, whether that is Shopify theme customisation for brands where the right premium theme provides a strong foundation, or full bespoke Shopify store builds for brands where the complexity of what they need cannot be served by a theme. Either way, the UX review is the foundation. The design that follows is grounded in evidence rather than assumption.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”791020″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”101686″]What a Shopify UX review typically surfaces[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”144892″]Every store is different, so every UX review surfaces its own set of findings. But there are common patterns I see often enough to be worth flagging:

  • Mobile-desktop design mismatch. Sites that work well on desktop but collapse on mobile, often because the design was built desktop-first and mobile was retrofitted.
  • Product cards that hide important information. One of the highest-impact components on any ecommerce site, and one of the most frequent culprits. I have written more about this in my article on Shopify product card design.
  • Checkout flows where customers cannot tell what step they are on, or where the call-to-action is buried below other content that distracts from the next step.
  • Homepages that bury the most-clicked content below the fold, because the team prioritised brand storytelling over what customers actually want to do on the site.
  • Trust signals missing from the moments they matter most, especially at the product page and the checkout, where customers are deciding whether to commit.
  • Inconsistent design language across the site, where the homepage feels considered but the collection page or the cart looks like a different brand designed it.
  • Mobile fold issues, where critical content or CTAs sit below the fold on common phone viewports and customers never scroll to find them.

The case studies I have published show what happens after these findings get addressed. The Drink Finder case study, Fuzzball case study, Hartnack & Co case study, and Thameen London case study all started with the same UX review process described above. The design work that followed was grounded in what the review surfaced, and the conversion uplift each project achieved is the evidence that this way of working actually pays back.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”791020″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”175564″]Why this matters for your project[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”139906″]If you are about to start a Shopify project with a designer or an agency, the question to ask is simple. How are you going to start? If the answer involves personas, brand workshops, and discovery sessions before anyone has looked at the analytics, you are paying for a comfort blanket rather than a foundation.

A UX review grounded in real data is not just a better starting point. It is also a faster one. By the time the design work begins, the priorities are clear, the evidence is documented, and every decision that follows has a reason behind it that goes beyond personal preference. That clarity protects the project from the worst kind of design work — the kind where someone redesigns something because they think it should look different, with no evidence that it was a problem in the first place.

It also makes the work I do measurable. Every Shopify CRO change I recommend can be tied back to a specific finding on the Miro board. Every design decision has a real-user justification. The client gets a clear story for why each change is being made, and the team has a clear yardstick for whether the change worked once the new site is live.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”791020″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”861312″]How the UX review fits into a Shopify project[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”140163″]To be clear, the UX review is not a standalone deliverable I sell on its own. It is how I start every project. Whether the engagement is a Shopify theme customisation, a bespoke Shopify store build, a Shopify migration, or Shopify design for DTC brands more broadly, the UX review is the foundation everything else is built on.

This matters commercially because it means the review is in your project budget by default, not an additional cost on top. It also means I do not have an incentive to identify problems that justify selling a separate review service. The work is the work. The review is part of it because it produces better design outcomes, not because it inflates the invoice.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”390829″][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][vc_column column_width_percent=”100″ gutter_size=”4″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”6/12″ uncode_shortcode_id=”191092″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/1″][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”181566″]Real users beat invented ones every time[/vc_custom_heading][vc_column_text uncode_shortcode_id=”192633″]The persona approach is comfortable. It produces a tidy slide deck, it fills a discovery phase, and it gives everyone in the room a sense that they understand the user. But the understanding is invented. The real customers, the ones who matter, are already on the live site. Their behaviour is already in the analytics. Their journey is already mappable. Looking at imagined users first, and pretending the real ones do not exist until later, is the wrong way round.

Every Shopify project I take on starts with a UX review because the alternative is starting with assumptions. Real users, real journeys, real data, real design judgment applied to a real store. text_color_type=”uncode-palette”]A Shopify UX review is a structured analysis of how customers actually use a live Shopify store, combining real GA4 analytics data with designer judgement to identify where the experience is helping conversion and where it is hurting it. It covers the full purchase journey from landing on the site to completing checkout, flags both what is working and what is not, and produces a clear set of design priorities.[/vc_column_text][/vc_accordion_tab][vc_accordion_tab gutter_size=”3″ column_padding=”2″ title=”How is a UX review different from a generic ecommerce audit?” tab_id=”1753877405-2-3015d5-517d4844-077a2e8a-a352″][vc_column_text text_color=”color-nhtu” uncode_shortcode_id=”563976″ text_color_type=”uncode-palette”]A generic ecommerce audit usually checks a site against a fixed list of best practices like page speed, CTA visibility, and mobile responsiveness. A proper UX review is grounded in real user data from GA4, maps the actual customer journey on the actual screens those customers are using, and applies design judgement to the specific store rather than measuring it against a generic checklist.[/vc_column_text][/vc_accordion_tab][vc_accordion_tab gutter_size=”3″ column_padding=”2″ title=”What data is used in a Shopify UX review?” tab_id=”1753883631279-2-815d5-517d4844-077a2e8a-a352″][vc_column_text text_color=”color-nhtu” uncode_shortcode_id=”201638″ text_color_type=”uncode-palette”]

GA4 reports including Traffic Acquisition, Landing Pages, Pages and Screens, Organic Search queries, User Demographics, Tech (device, OS, browser), Resolution by revenue, Purchase Journey, and Ecommerce purchases. The goal is a topline picture of who is using the store, on what devices, on which pages, and where they drop out of the funnel, not a deep analytics dive.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_accordion_tab][vc_accordion_tab gutter_size=”3″ column_padding=”2″ title=”Do I need a UX review before redesigning my Shopify store?” tab_id=”1753883631279-2-815d5-517d4844-077a2e8a-a3522″][vc_column_text text_color=”color-nhtu” uncode_shortcode_id=”230470″ text_color_type=”uncode-palette”]Yes. Redesigning a Shopify store without a UX review means designing on assumption rather than evidence. Even when the design problems seem obvious, real-user data often surfaces priorities that contradict the team’s instincts. A UX review takes a fraction of the project budget and consistently saves time and rework later.[/vc_column_text][/vc_accordion_tab][vc_accordion_tab gutter_size=”3″ column_padding=”2″ title=”Why not just use personas instead?” tab_id=”1753883631279-2-815d5-517d4844-077a2e8a-a35227″][vc_column_text text_color=”color-nhtu” uncode_shortcode_id=”140252″ text_color_type=”uncode-palette”]Personas are fictional users invented from assumption rather than evidence. For brand-new products with no customers yet, they can be a reasonable starting point. For an established Shopify store with real customers and real analytics already running, building personas instead of looking at the real users is choosing imagined data over real data, which is rarely a good design decision.[/vc_column_text][/vc_accordion_tab][vc_accordion_tab gutter_size=”3″ column_padding=”2″ title=”Do you charge separately for a UX review?” tab_id=”1753883631279-2-815d5-517d4844-077a2e8a-a352276″][vc_column_text text_color=”color-nhtu” uncode_shortcode_id=”150559″ text_color_type=”uncode-palette”]The UX review is included in the scope of every Shopify project I take on rather than being charged for as a separate service. The deliverables, the shared Miro board and the itemised to-do list with design and development time allocations, feed directly into the design and development scope for the rest of the project, so it makes more sense to keep them as part of the same engagement. Get in touch to talk through your project and I can give you a clear scope and cost based on what your store actually needs.[/vc_column_text][/vc_accordion_tab][vc_accordion_tab gutter_size=”3″ column_padding=”2″ title=”Is a UX review a standalone service?” tab_id=”1753883631279-2-815d5-517d4844-077a2e8a-a3522764″][vc_column_text text_color=”color-nhtu” uncode_shortcode_id=”784222″ text_color_type=”uncode-palette”]Not in my work. The output is a shared Miro board the client keeps, plus a to-do list with design and development time allocations against each item, so the client can prioritise what gets done first based on their budget and their commercial priorities.[/vc_column_text][/vc_accordion_tab][/vc_accordion][/vc_column][vc_column width=”3/12″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”5″ top_padding=”2″ bottom_padding=”2″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”209535″][vc_column width=”1/1″][vc_separator sep_color=”color-gyho” uncode_shortcode_id=”612153″ sep_color_type=”uncode-palette”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column width=”1/1″][uncode_block id=”2834″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row row_height_percent=”0″ override_padding=”yes” h_padding=”2″ top_padding=”5″ bottom_padding=”3″ overlay_alpha=”50″ gutter_size=”3″ column_width_percent=”100″ shift_y=”0″ z_index=”0″ content_parallax=”0″ uncode_shortcode_id=”835762″][vc_column column_width_use_pixel=”yes” position_vertical=”middle” align_horizontal=”align_center” gutter_size=”3″ overlay_alpha=”50″ shift_x=”0″ shift_y=”0″ shift_y_down=”0″ z_index=”0″ medium_width=”0″ mobile_width=”0″ width=”1/1″ uncode_shortcode_id=”112835″ column_width_pixel=”750px”][vc_custom_heading uncode_shortcode_id=”145284″]Let’s create your Shopify success story[/vc_custom_heading]

excerpt.rendered: A Shopify UX review is where every project should start, and yet most agencies skip it in favour of made-up personas and assumptions. This article walks through what a real UX review involves — GA4 data analysis, Miro purchase journey mapping, and heuristic design review — and why working from real users beats inventing imaginary ones every time.

mainEntity.name: What is a Shopify UX review?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Shopify UX review is a structured analysis of how customers actually use a live Shopify store, combining real GA4 analytics data with designer judgement to identify where the experience is helping conversion and where it is hurting it. It covers the full purchase journey from landing on the site to completing checkout, flags both what is working and what is not, and produces a clear set of design priorities.

mainEntity.name: How is a UX review different from a generic ecommerce audit?

acceptedAnswer.text: A generic ecommerce audit usually checks a site against a fixed list of best practices like page speed, CTA visibility, and mobile responsiveness. A proper UX review is grounded in real user data from GA4, maps the actual customer journey on the actual screens those customers are using, and applies design judgement to the specific store rather than measuring it against a generic checklist.

mainEntity.name: What data is used in a Shopify UX review?

acceptedAnswer.text: GA4 reports including Traffic Acquisition, Landing Pages, Pages and Screens, Organic Search queries, User Demographics, Tech (device, OS, browser), Resolution by revenue, Purchase Journey, and Ecommerce purchases. The goal is a topline picture of who is using the store, on what devices, on which pages, and where they drop out of the funnel, not a deep analytics dive.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a UX review before redesigning my Shopify store?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Redesigning a Shopify store without a UX review means designing on assumption rather than evidence. Even when the design problems seem obvious, real-user data often surfaces priorities that contradict the team's instincts. A UX review takes a fraction of the project budget and consistently saves time and rework later.

mainEntity.name: Why not just use personas instead?

acceptedAnswer.text: Personas are fictional users invented from assumption rather than evidence. For brand-new products with no customers yet, they can be a reasonable starting point. For an established Shopify store with real customers and real analytics already running, building personas instead of looking at the real users is choosing imagined data over real data.

mainEntity.name: Do you charge separately for a UX review?

acceptedAnswer.text: The UX review is included in the scope of every Shopify project rather than being charged for as a separate service. The deliverables, the shared Miro board and the itemised to-do list with design and development time allocations, feed directly into the design and development scope for the rest of the project, so it makes more sense to keep them as part of the same engagement.

mainEntity.name: Is a UX review a standalone service?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not in this practice. The UX review is how every Shopify project begins, so it is included in the project scope by default rather than sold as a separate deliverable. The output is a shared Miro board the client keeps, plus a to-do list with design and development time allocations against each item, so the client can prioritise what gets done first.
